name: Uma Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the tills at Marlow's, the big supermarket on Canal Street, mostly the early shift from six till two. I open till four, count my float, and then it's scanning, bagging help, price checks and people asking where the gravy is. I've been there just over a year and I'm still slow on the loose fruit codes, so the queue builds behind me on a Saturday. The best bit is the regulars, like old Mr Adeyemi who comes in every Tuesday for one tin of sardines and a chat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My feet and the self-checkout bay wear me out, honestly. When I'm put on the bay I'm basically a human error message, running between six machines that all beep at once. What keeps me there is the pay, because our union got us a better rate than the other chains, and the people. Tomás, my partner, drives buses, and between us we've put away about nine months of living costs, so I'm not scared of a bad week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the break room: told you so. Everyone was panicking about robots, and the shop got slightly smarter scales that know a banana from a pear. I'd probably post something smug in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays my job. The routine bits that change are mostly the stock ordering in the back office, which I never touch anyway. I'd still worry a little about the self-checkout bay growing, because management loves that bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and finally learn the fruit codes properly, because that's my real problem, not AI. I'd keep paying my union dues and go to the branch meeting in March. Tomás and I would keep putting a bit aside each month like we already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit silly for worrying, maybe. It feels like the world I know, which is the world I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the self-checkout bay. If it grew by a few machines even in this world, who on your shift would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Janice, who's been on the tills nineteen years and hates the bay even more than me. Janice can't stand the beeping and her knees are bad, so standing at the bay all shift would finish her. I'd want the union to make sure people like her keep a staffed till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd spend your savings on if things stayed this steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a holiday, a real one, which we haven't had in three years. Tomás wants to go see his family. In this world I'd feel fine spending a chunk of it, because the job isn't going anywhere.

say: I told everyone the **robot panic** was overblown, and the smarter fruit scales prove it.
I'd post in the **union chat** that our tills are safe for now.
think: My **job stays mine**, because the changes land in the back office, not on my till.
The **self-checkout bay** still bothers me, because management likes it more than staffed tills.
do: Learn the **fruit codes** properly so the Saturday queue stops building behind me.
Go to the union **branch meeting** in March and keep paying dues.
Keep saving monthly with Tomás and maybe spend some on a **family holiday**.
feel: **Relieved** and a little silly for worrying.
Comfortable, because this is the **familiar world** I like.
S0.quote: Everyone was panicking about robots, and the shop got slightly smarter scales that know a banana from a pear.
fieldNote: Her real worry here is her **own speed** on the till, not technology.
She judges change through **older colleagues** like Janice before herself.
Savings make her **relaxed** enough to plan a holiday in this world.

steps.text: Learn the loose fruit codes to speed up Saturday queues
Attend the union branch meeting in March
Book a trip to visit Tomás's family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union. If the office stuff goes to software and the bay keeps growing, someone has to make sure people aren't just dumped. I'd share the union's petition and argue with my cousin who thinks it's all progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My actual till work changes slowly, because robots are slow in this picture. But the phone line and the online orders team at Marlow's would shrink, and those people would want my shifts. So I'd be competing with nicer, faster people for fewer staffed tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up as a workplace contact for the union in the first few months, because I'd rather be inside the fight than read about it. I'd ask my manager, Dev, for more shop floor shifts instead of the bay. I'd keep the savings untouched and skip the holiday for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't love change, and this is change creeping in sideways. My job's fine today, but the ground's moving under the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. If Marlow's asked you to use an AI headset to answer customer questions, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, but I'd probably do it if it was that or the bay. I'd want the union to check what it records about us. I don't want a computer counting my bathroom breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if jobs shrink in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bosses at head office, not the machines. A machine doesn't decide to cut hours, a spreadsheet person at head office does. Governments too, if they let it happen with no rules.

say: I'd say this is exactly why we need a **strong union** with a say on new technology.
I'd share the **union petition** and argue with family who call it progress.
think: My till changes **slowly**, but office staff would come looking for **shop floor shifts**.
I'd be competing with **faster people** for fewer staffed tills.
do: Sign up as a **union workplace contact** in the first few months.
Ask my manager Dev for **shop floor shifts** instead of the self-checkout bay.
Leave the **savings untouched** and skip the holiday for a year.
feel: **Uneasy**, because change is creeping in sideways.
Safe today, but watching **the ground move** under others.
S1.quote: A machine doesn't decide to cut hours, a spreadsheet person at head office does.
fieldNote: She blames **head office** and weak rules, never the machines themselves.
Her answer to change is **collective**, not personal retraining.
She would accept an **AI headset** only as the lesser evil.

steps.text: Volunteer as the union's workplace contact at Marlow's
Ask manager Dev for shop floor shifts over the bay
Skip next year's holiday and leave the savings alone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs a law, now, before 2031. Thinking AI by 2028 hits the office people, but robots by 2031 hit me and every Janice in the country. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd tell anyone online to call their representatives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's gone by 2031 and I have no backup. I'm not techy and I never wanted to be. The savings would carry us a while, but a while isn't a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go to every union and community meeting and push for a job guarantee or retraining paid by the companies. I'd keep working every shift I can and save harder, maybe a third of my pay. I'd look at care work, because a robot holding someone's hand at a care home feels far off even then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. The kind that sits in your stomach at three in the morning. And angry that nobody asked us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have more savings than most people on the tills. Does that change how scared you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys time, not a plan. Nine months of savings goes quickly if my partner's buses get robot drivers too. Nine months would feel like a countdown rather than a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mr Adeyemi, the Tuesday regular, about the tills going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mr Adeyemi I was sorry, and that I'd try to visit him. He comes for the chat as much as the sardines. Nobody's going to build a robot that asks about his late wife.

say: I'd demand a **law before 2031**, because robots then hit every till worker.
I'd tell people online to **call their representatives** and join a union.
think: My **job is gone** by 2031, and I have no backup skills.
Our **nine months** of savings buy time, not a career.
do: Push at **union meetings** for company-paid retraining or a job guarantee.
Save about **a third** of my pay while the tills still need me.
Look into **care work**, which feels further from robots.
feel: **Scared** in a way that keeps me awake at three in the morning.
**Angry** that nobody asked till workers first.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings goes quickly if my partner's buses get robot drivers too.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** and says so plainly.
The **3-year gap** before robots is her only window, and she uses it for organising.
Care work appeals because it keeps **human contact**, which she values most.

steps.text: Push the union for company-paid retraining before 2031
Save a third of each pay packet into the joint account
Ask the local care home about part-time shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not enough time for the government to do anything right, so we have to start now. I'd keep going on about the union and decent rules. I'd probably bore my friends about it at the pub quiz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get till about 2034 on the tills, which is a bit more breathing room. But I'm still not someone who jumps into new things. I'd probably waste the first two years hoping it wouldn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself do one thing a year, because otherwise I'd do nothing. This year I'd go to the union's training day on workers' rights. Next year I'd try a care certificate at the college on weekends, and keep saving the same steady amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but not frozen. Five years feels like a long time until you count it in Christmases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste two years hoping. What would actually push you to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first robot shelf stacker at Marlow's. Once something is in my shop it's real to me, and before that it's news. Tomás says I need to see a thing before I believe it, and he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra time change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about buying a flat in a few years. I think we'd still do it, but smaller, so the mortgage doesn't sink us if I'm out of work. Tomás would say go for it, I'd say go small.

say: I'd say **five years** is too short for governments, so unions must **start now**.
I'd keep pushing **decent rules** on friends at the pub quiz.
think: I get roughly until **2034** on the tills, which is some breathing room.
I'd probably **waste two years** hoping it wouldn't happen.
do: Attend the union's **workers' rights** training day this year.
Start a weekend **care certificate** at the college next year.
Keep saving the **same amount** and plan a smaller flat.
feel: Five years feels long until I count it in **Christmases**.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a long time until you count it in Christmases.
fieldNote: She knows she **delays** and builds a one-thing-a-year rule to beat it.
Change only feels real once it's **inside her shop**.
Housing plans shrink to a **smaller flat** as a hedge.

steps.text: Attend the union's workers' rights training day this year
Enrol in a weekend care certificate at the college
Choose a smaller flat so one wage covers the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse for bosses or governments. I'd want a plan with real money in it for people like me. I'd say it at union meetings and at family dinners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm 37 when the robots come for the tills. That's young enough to start again, but I'd have to actually start. I'd still be uneasy, because I'm not good at starting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Marlow's for a few more years and move up to a supervisor role if they'd have me. I'd do the care certificate slowly, maybe one module a year. And I'd keep saving, because money is the one thing I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the fast ones. Still a knot, but a small one. Like knowing an exam is far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push for anything specific, given a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want a rule. A shop shouldn't take out staffed tills without retraining the people on them, and one staffed till should stay open for old folks. Mr Adeyemi would need it. That one's not even about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said supervisor. Do you think you'd get there, still learning the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not soon, I'm honest about that. I'm still the one who gets the fruit codes wrong. But in ten years even I'd learn them.

say: I'd say a **decade** leaves bosses and governments **no excuse** for a bad plan.
I'd argue for **real money** for retraining at union meetings and family dinners.
think: I'd be **37** when robots reach the tills, young enough to start again.
I'm **not good at starting** things, which is my real risk.
do: Stay at Marlow's and aim for a **supervisor role** within a few years.
Take the **care certificate** one module a year.
Keep **saving steadily**, the one thing I'm already good at.
feel: Like knowing an **exam** is still far off.
S4.quote: A shop shouldn't take out staffed tills without retraining the people on them, and one staffed till should stay open for old folks.
fieldNote: Even with a decade she rates her **own inertia** as the main threat.
Her policy ideas protect **older customers** as well as workers.
Saving is her **comfort zone**, and she leans on it.

steps.text: Apply for a shift supervisor role at Marlow's
Complete one care certificate module each year
Campaign for a staffed-till rule through the union

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because robots by 2031 means the tills go before I've done anything. What would help is a law that makes shops pay for retraining before they bring robots in, and a union strong enough to enforce it. And someone telling me, plainly, which jobs are still safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about customers. Half of my regulars come for the talk, and nobody's counting that. If the tills go, a lot of lonely people lose their one chat of the day.

headlineQuote: If the tills go, a lot of lonely people lose their one chat of the day.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old cashier** at a big supermarket, still slow on the fruit codes after a year.
She and her partner Tomás have **nine months saved**, and union pay keeps her above other chains.
She never uses AI and **dislikes change**, admitting she'd waste time hoping it passes.
She stays calm in **AI Plateau**, grows uneasy in Steady Disruption, and is **alarmed** by AGI by 2028.
Her answer to every scenario is the **union** and rules, plus a slow move toward care work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots by 2031 take the tills before she has a plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** making shops pay for retraining before robots arrive.
Plain advice on which **jobs stay safe**.
